It is known that in the mid-19th century, approximately 40,000 slaves passed through Zanzibar annually.
Those who survived these inhumane conditions were put up for auction.
What shocked me most was the fact that the slave trade was abolished by order of the Sultan only at the end of the 19th century, in 1873!
Zanzibar was under Portuguese rule from the late 15th century until 1698, when the island was taken over by the Sultans of Oman.
According to historians' estimates, between 1830 and 1873, approximately 600,000 people were sold here as merchandise, and many more slaves were held here en route to their destinations.
In 1861, Zanzibar became a British colony.
By then, many activists were campaigning for the abolition of slavery.
Zanzibar seceded from the British Empire in 1963.
In January 1964, a revolution took place, resulting in the country becoming the independent Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba.
Three months later, in April of that year, it formed a new state – Tanzania – with the Republic of Tanganyika, while retaining significant autonomy (including a separate government and president).

The Freddie Mercury Museum: A Bittersweet Disappointment
As a Freddie Mercury fan, my visit to the museum left me with mixed feelings, leaning towards disappointment.
While it's exciting to have a space dedicated to a legend like him, the experience is marred by two major problems.
The first, and most hurtful, is the hypocrisy of a museum celebrating the life of a gay icon like Freddie existing and profiting in a country where homosexuality is prohibited and criminalized.
It's an unacceptable contradiction that borders on exploitation, and as a fan and a gay man, it fills me with deep indignation.
How is it possible that they profit from his legacy while people are persecuted and oppressed for being who they are in this country?
This situation completely overshadows any positive aspects of the visit.
Furthermore, the museum is expensive for what it offers.
The collection is quite limited and doesn't justify the entrance fee.
The value for money is poor, which only intensifies the feeling that they're exploiting Freddie's name without offering anything worthy of him.
In short, for me it was a bittersweet and somewhat frustrating experience.

As soon as you start questioning the ethical aspects of the whole thing, you're immediately told that it's a "rescue center"—which is simply a blatant lie.
We were told that this was practically impossible.
The animals clearly have no wounds or other externally visible problems; they can't be sick either, since sick animals in the wild are almost always infested with parasites.
This means that, for obvious reasons, it's not allowed for random tourists to enter the water with these animals.
Then we were told that the animals are released again and again – after we asked several times and expressed our concerns, we were given a few more facts.
The turtles that end up in these "caves" are bycatch.
They then serve as tourist attractions for a while until, under a grand guise of "animal welfare," they are released back into their natural habitat.
In short: after a few minutes of discussion, we left immediately and asked for a refund (15 dollars is easily a full day's budget for backpackers), which, of course, we didn't receive.
Please, in the name of animal welfare, do not support such facilities!

Disappointed is the word.
My visit to Zanzibar has been a profound disappointment, far removed from the idyllic image it usually projects.
The experience has been marked by a series of negative points that have left me with a constant feeling of frustration and, at times, of being ripped off.
This duplication of expenses is, to say the least, unjustifiable and makes you feel like you're being taken advantage of from the very beginning.
The island is extremely dirty, with plastic and trash everywhere.
The beaches, which should be the main attraction, are sadly polluted, marring the landscape and making the experience of enjoying them unpleasant.
It's truly shocking to see such a level of environmental neglect in a place that depends on tourism.
Furthermore, the feeling of being constantly ripped off is palpable.
Prices for tourists are blatantly higher than for locals, making you feel exploited in every transaction, from buying a simple souvenir to haggling over a service or taking the bus.
To get from Stone Town to Nungwi, I was charged 10,000 tzh one way, while it costs locals 2,500, and then 5,000 tzh the return trip.
It makes no sense.
While food in restaurants can be affordable, eating on the street is a gamble and often results in being financially ripped off.
However, even this is overshadowed by their constant push to sell you something, which, while understandable in a tourist context, can become exhausting.
Compared to my experience on the Tanzanian mainland, where I felt much more comfortable and at ease, Zanzibar didn't give me that sense of home or authenticity.
I definitely feel let down and I, for one, will not be returning.

clause_text: Another sad part about the slave trading history.
Access was impossible, it was closed and no one was there to open it for us…
This place was a secret slave imprisonment and transit point set up by slave traders on the island after the slave trade was banned.

The story is very sad.
Slaves were brought into the semi-subterranean cellar, men on one side, women and children on the other.
They were kept in chains and loaded onto ships in the small bay, then shipped to Mombasa, Kenya, to be sold.
About 15-20 minutes visit.
Between 1880-1905, the chamber was being used as a place of concealment of the human cargo pending their disposal.

I booked the sunset cruise and the Mnemba Island tour, and both were absolutely unforgettable.
Unfortunately, this tour was a huge disappointment.
The organization was disastrous: Upon pickup, we were quickly charged, shoved onto some random bus, and then disappeared.
We had no idea what was going on.
There was no plan for who to contact or anything else.
After a few minutes, the bus stopped at a gas station without informing the passengers.
In the end, everyone had to wait 25 minutes simply because two passengers were booked on a different tour.
The bus driver drove like a maniac, completely disregarding safety.
Several times we were genuinely afraid of an accident.
The boats were truly dilapidated and in terrible condition.
It was as if their motto was "as long as they don't sink." Seasickness sufferers were already at their wits' end here, as the boats crawled across the sea at a snail's pace, causing extreme rocking.
The island itself is run-down, overcrowded, and not very appealing.
Afterwards, we went to the Nakupenda sandbank.
Instead of a dream island with clear water, it was overcrowded, with greenish-murky water, and vendors constantly pestered the guests, even while eating.
Leftovers from lunch were even lying around on the beach (e.g., shrimp heads).
Shady spots consisted of makeshift blankets.
As an alternative, there was chicken – unfortunately inedible: My girlfriend got a small piece with meat, I only got bones with skin and cartilage.
We weren't full.
The return trip was also chaotic: A couple who had already kept everyone waiting were late again.
The boat left without them, had to turn around, and the man completely lost it – aggressive, insulting, almost violent towards the guide.
Very unpleasant for all the other passengers.
In conclusion: A pure mass-market experience with no quality.

As an alternative, they told us we could swim there since the boat couldn't get close, which isn't a realistic or safe option for everyone, and in practice, we didn't see anything.

A pristine island?

A SERIOUS SAFETY WARNING: Negligent, Dangerous, and Life-Threatening Experience
I am writing this review as a formal complaint and a serious warning to any individual or family considering using Zanzibar Water Sports for an excursion.
Our experience was not merely disappointing; it was life-threatening due to the company's gross negligence and complete disregard for customer safety.
We were led to believe the trip was organised through our hotel, only to discover it was operated by this external company.
The booking process was unprofessional; we received only a paper slip, with no formal documentation, no safety briefing, and no health and safety checks conducted before we left the shore.
This initial lack of protocol was a clear indicator of the dangers to come.
The situation escalated dramatically when we were taken to a second location to see dolphins.
The staff rushed us, telling us to hurriedly put on our gear and get in the water.
Feeling pressured, I entered the water as instructed while the boat's engine was off.
To my horror, the moment I surfaced, the driver started the engine.
I was immediately swept under the boat and pulled into the current created by the moving vessel.
I was fully submerged, drowning and fighting for my life as the boat drove directly over me.
The propellers passed inches from my head and body before striking my ankle, cutting it down to the bone.
After screaming for the driver to stop, I managed to swim back to the boat.
The complete lack of preparedness was appalling
* No First Aid Kit: There was absolutely no first aid kit on board.
My severe, bleeding wound had to be bandaged with a t-shirt.
* No Emergency Training: The staff showed no signs of first aid training or any ability to handle a medical emergency.
* A Negligent Return Journey: I was forced to endure a 40-minute boat journey back to the hotel while actively bleeding and showing clear signs of shock, with no medical assistance offered.
Upon our return, the situation did not improve, and we had to take our own private taxi to a hospital for professional medical treatment, which included stitches and an X-ray.
This was not an unfortunate accident; it was the direct and predictable result of a company operating with a shocking level of negligence.
The key failures include
* Failure to provide any safety briefing.
* Reckless and dangerous operation of the boat.
* Failure to ensure the area around the propeller was clear before starting the engine.
* Failure to carry basic, essential safety equipment like a first aid kit.
This company's conduct is a danger to the public.

In 1919 the British governor of Seychelles sent a gift of four Aldabra giant tortoises to Changuu from the island of Aldabra.
However people began to steal the tortoises for sale abroad as pets or for food and their numbers dropped rapidly.
By 1988 there were around 100 tortoises, fifty in 1990 and just seven by 1996.
A further 80 hatchlings were taken to the island in 1996 to increase the numbers but 40 of them vanished.

The Zanzibar government, with assistance from the World Society for the Protection of Animals (Now known as World Animal Protection) built a large compound for the protection of the animals and by 2000 numbers had recovered to 17 adults, 50 juveniles and 90 hatchlings.
The species is now considered vulnerable and has been placed on the IUCN Red List by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
